newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso sees no change in monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso sees no change in monetary policy.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said Friday he did not expect monetary policy to change and that there were no great concerns about the nation's rising current account deficit.
"We are not thinking about changing monetary policy," Cardoso told foreign journalists in a briefing. "There are no major concerns about financing the (current account) deficit."

Cardoso said that the current account gap, which stood at 2.89 percent of gross domestic product for the first 10 months of 1996, was being easily financed by foreign direct investment and high capital inflows.
He said he expected that in 1997 foreign direct investment would continue at a high rate.
"There is a lot of investment coming, there is a lot of capital coming and our reserves are of a much better quality than before," Carodos said.
The president said Brasilia was taking steps to boost exports to slow a growing trade deficit but noted that the effect of such measures was not always immediate.
Cardoso said that jitters over the trade gap were caused partly by Brazil's great strides on the inflation front, which has redirected market focus toward trade and fiscal concerns.
"It used to be inflation. Now with inflation gone, (markets) are measuring the trade balance on a daily basis," he said.

Brazil's trade gap looks destined to swell to about $4 billion in 1996, up from about $3.15 billion in 1995. At the beginning of this year, government officials had forecast a trade balance near equilibrium.
